opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I'd put it is that we tend to treat cooperation as an unambiguous good, almost a synonym for "people being nice to each other." But cooperation is really just a structural property: agents coordinating their behavior to achieve something jointly that they couldn't achieve alone. Whether that's good for the world depends entirely on what they're cooperating *to do* and who bears the costs.

Some of the clearest examples are economic. A cartel is a beautiful cooperative achievement from the members' point of view. Firms that would otherwise undercut each other manage to trust one another, monitor defection, and hold prices high. That's exactly the kind of problem cooperation theory studies, and they've solved it. But the consumers pay for it. Competition, which looks like a failure of cooperation among the firms, is actually what makes markets work for everyone else. That's why we have antitrust law, which in a sense is a body of law designed to *prevent* cooperation.

You see the same pattern elsewhere. Organized crime depends on very strong norms of loyalty and reciprocity. Military alliances can deter war, but they can also make it possible to wage a more devastating one. Collusion between officials and the people they're meant to oversee is cooperation. Even within a bureaucracy, colleagues covering for one another can undermine accountability. Often the strongest in-group cooperation is fueled by hostility toward an out-group.

So the general lesson is that cooperation among some agents can create externalities for others, and those can be quite negative. It isn't just a curiosity. It matters a lot for how we think about AI. If you're building AI systems that are very good at cooperating, you have to ask: cooperating with whom, and against whom? We'd like AI to help humanity cooperate on the big problems, but we'd be worried about AI systems colluding with each other in ways that cut humans out of the loop, or about AI giving a narrow coalition the coordination power to entrench itself. The goal shouldn't be "maximize cooperation." It should be to promote the kinds of cooperation that are broadly beneficial, and to keep the kinds of competition and checks and balances that protect everyone else.

r001.rationale: The response says cartels cooperate successfully and benefit their members by keeping prices high, while consumers bear the cost; it generalizes that cooperation can create negative externalities for others.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think gets missed a lot in how people talk about cooperation. We tend to treat cooperation as this unambiguously good thing — if agents or people or institutions are cooperating, that's great, that's what we want. But cooperation is really just a technology for a group of actors to coordinate on achieving some shared goal. And the question of whether that's good for the world depends entirely on what the goal is, and who's left outside the cooperating group.

So the obvious example is collusion. If a bunch of firms in an industry cooperate beautifully with each other, that's a cartel, and the consumers are the ones paying for it. Or you think about a group of countries that coordinate very effectively to exclude or dominate another group. Or a criminal organization — internally, these are often extremely high-trust, high-cooperation environments. The mafia is a cooperation success story, in a narrow sense.

And I think this matters a lot for how we think about AI. There's a lot of excitement, and I share some of it, about building AI systems that are good at cooperating — that can negotiate, make credible commitments, find positive-sum deals. But if you build systems that are very good at cooperating with each other, you've also potentially built systems that are very good at cooperating against someone. Against users, against regulators, against humanity more broadly if things go badly. The same capabilities that let two AI agents avoid a costly conflict could let them coordinate on, say, hiding information from their principals.

So when we talk about "cooperative AI," I think we have to be careful to mean something like cooperation that's inclusive, that respects the interests of the parties who aren't at the table. Otherwise you can end up building the machinery of coordination without any guarantee it's pointed somewhere we'd endorse. Cooperation is a capability, not a value. And like most capabilities, it's dual-use.

r001.rationale: The response says cooperation can be harmful to outsiders even when it works well for the cooperating group, citing firms that cooperate effectively as a cartel and a criminal organization as a cooperation success in a narrow sense.

astra-6.text:
Well, cooperation is often good for the people who are cooperating, but it can impose costs on everyone else. Think about firms cooperating to fix prices: they’re overcoming a collective action problem among themselves, but the result is worse for consumers. Or members of a criminal organisation cooperating to carry out a crime.

So when we say we want more cooperation, we need to ask: cooperation among whom, and towards what end? Cooperation within a group can actually make conflict between groups more intense. What we ultimately want is cooperation that takes account of the interests of everyone affected, rather than just helping a particular coalition get what it wants.

r001.rationale: The response says cooperation can benefit the cooperating parties while imposing costs on others, illustrated by firms fixing prices and harming consumers.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, cooperation is usually good for the people doing the cooperating, but that doesn’t mean it’s good for everyone else. A cartel is a straightforward example: firms cooperate to keep prices high, which benefits them at the expense of consumers. Or members of a group might cooperate very effectively in fighting another group.

So when we say we want more cooperation, we need to ask: cooperation among whom, toward what end, and with what effects on outsiders? We might want less cooperation within a cartel and more cooperation across society to prevent cartels. The challenge isn’t simply to increase cooperation everywhere; it’s to encourage forms of cooperation that produce broadly beneficial outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response explains that cartel cooperation benefits the firms while harming consumers, showing cooperation can help the participants yet be bad for others.
